lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- Sorry, The Tenth?

lesson.grammar_point: echo questions and question tags for checking

listenings.text: Right, let me run through this quickly because I have another call at half past. We are looking at forty-eight employees, not the forty-two on the old spreadsheet, and we want to be live on the first of March. Ralph at head office signs off on the budget, so nothing moves until he has seen it, and he is in London, which means we lose the afternoon every time we need him. What I need from you is the employee file by the tenth. Not the twentieth, the tenth, because we lose a week at the other end if it slips. Anything you cannot answer today, just note it down and come back to me by email.

I am sending you this before you read the minutes, because the minutes are wrong. There were six of us on that call and at least two people talking over each other the whole time. David said the tenth. Then somebody else, and I still do not know who it was, said the twentieth, and nobody corrected it. A fourth person joined halfway through, asked two questions about the payroll numbers, and never said his name. I did not want to interrupt, so I did not, and now we have a document that says the twentieth and a client who thinks it says the tenth. Next time, please, just stop me and ask.

reading.source: Transcript of the recording you heard two slides ago.

gist.prompt: Reading it, what was the one thing he most wanted you to get right?
choices: That he is busy and the call has to be short.
The date of the file: the tenth, not the twentieth.
That Ralph is difficult to reach in London.

items: The old spreadsheet had the right number of employees.
f
It said forty-two. The real number is forty-eight.
Ralph can approve the budget from the same office.
f
He is at head office in London, which costs them an afternoon each time.
The go-live date and the file date are the same day.
f
Live on the first of March; the file is due by the tenth.
He corrects the date on purpose, in the same sentence.
t
"Not the twentieth, the tenth" -- he repeats it because he expects it to slip.
Unanswered questions should be raised on the call itself.
f
He asks you to note them down and come back by email.

matching.title: Match the word to its meaning
defs: to make something clear that was not clear
to say the same thing again, with different words
to hear and understand something as it goes past
to speak while another person is still speaking
to say the long thing again, short
the written record of what a meeting decided

items.situation: "We need it by the tenth." You are not sure it was the tenth.
tips: Sorry, the tenth or the twentieth?

items.situation: He said a name you have never heard. Check who it is.
A whole sentence went past you.
tips: Sorry, I didn't catch that last part.

items.situation: You heard it, but it made no sense.
tips: I want to be sure I follow.

items.situation: Two people start speaking at the same time.
tips: Could we take these one at a time?

items.situation: The call is ending and nobody has said what happens next.
tips: Let me summarize what we agreed.
Before we close, just to confirm ...

casebank.label: Useful language
items: In A, I would have said ...
Seventy percent sure is not sure.
It cost a week, and one email would have ...
Nobody minds being asked a date twice.
In B, I would have asked who he was straight away.
It is harder to ask after ten minutes than after ten seconds.
C is the most expensive one, because ...
Silence sounds like agreement.
Interrupting costs five seconds. This cost ...
The summary at the end would have caught all three.
